label: Flowchart

edges.label: Topic 'Control flow' of section 1.3 holds the concept algorithm pseudocode.

[0] everyday_reading (E): Folk meaning: an everyday flowchart is a static picture or a decision tree read top to bottom once, so a novice reads a loop-back arrow as decoration and the diamond as a one-time question. In a program flowchart, each path is a possible execution, and an arrow returning to a diamond means the test is evaluated again.

[0] names_the_element (N): Diagram: a flowchart is a diagram of control flow. Boxes are statements, diamonds are boolean tests with yes/no exits, and arrows show the order of execution.
[1] states_the_rule (S): Every path through the flowchart corresponds to a flow-of-control path through the program. An if is a diamond whose branches rejoin; a while is a diamond whose yes branch runs the body and returns to the diamond.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Execution order: start at the entry; execute each box when reached; at a diamond evaluate the condition and follow the yes or no arrow; follow back arrows to re-test; stop at the exit.
[1] output_prediction (OP): The result of reading a flowchart for given inputs is the path taken (the sequence of boxes and branch choices) and so the output. For `if (x > y) max = x; else max = y;` with x = 2, y = 5, the path goes to the no branch and sets max = 5.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): One step moves along one arrow: either execute one box (changing the variables it assigns) or evaluate one diamond (changing nothing, choosing yes or no).

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): The flowchart's arrows are the program's control flow: sequence = a straight chain, if = branch and rejoin, loop = a back arrow to the test. Nesting a loop draws a loop inside a loop, and the diagram quickly becomes complex.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): Both describe an algorithm before it is code: a flowchart draws the flow of control as boxes and arrows, pseudocode writes the steps as English and Java text.
[2] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Purpose: to visualise and understand the control flow of basic building blocks (if, while, for) and to check where each path leads. It is not a way to design whole modern programs.

[0] predict_a_change (C): Moving the back arrow from the diamond to the body box changes a while into a do-while (test after). Removing the back arrow turns the loop into an if. Swapping the yes and no labels swaps the branches.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Use a flowchart to understand a single if, while, for or a small nesting. For larger programs, use indentation, traces and a limited set of structured constructs instead: flowcharts of complex control flow are hard to read.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A loop's back arrow must return to the test, not straight to the body. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Drawing or tracing the while body as repeating without re-checking the diamond: the body runs again after the condition is false.
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A diamond must have both yes and no exits. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Omitting the no path (e.g. for an if without else, or a loop exit): the diagram has no path for the false case.
Both describe an algorithm before it is code: a flowchart draws the flow of control as boxes and arrows, pseudocode writes the steps as English and Java text.
A flowchart draws the flow of control: each path through the diagram is a path the program can take.
